PART 5 — Revenge, Punishment, Justice and Restoration

5.1 Four Things Often Called "Justice"

Read the diagram carefully. It does not say consequences are wrong. It says the four things differ in who acts and what they aim at, and that the biblical vocabulary of justice leans toward the right-hand column while still assigning a role to the lower-left (Part 5.5).

5.2 The Biblical Vocabulary of Justice

WordLanguageMeaningWhere
מִשְׁפָּט mishpatHebrewJustice, judgment, the right ordering of a matter; in the prophets, repeatedly oriented to defending the vulnerableIsa 1:17 ("seek justice, correct oppression, bring justice to the fatherless, plead the widow's cause"); Mic 6:8; Amos 5:24
צְדָקָה tsedaqahHebrewRighteousness; right relationship and conduct within a covenant communityIsa 5:7 — God "looked for justice (mishpat) but behold, bloodshed (mispach); for righteousness (tsedaqah), but behold, an outcry (tse'aqah)" — a wordplay in which the missing justice is heard as the victims' cry
חֶסֶד chesedHebrewSteadfast covenant love, loyal kindnessMic 6:8: do justice, love chesed, walk humbly
נָקַם naqam / שִׁלֵּם shillemHebrewVengeance / recompense. The word for repay shares the root of shalom (wholeness), which at least invites the question whether biblical recompense is about balancing pain or completing and making whole (not every scholar draws theological weight from this)Deut 32:35 ("Vengeance is mine, and recompense")
δικαιοσύνη dikaiosyneGreekRighteousness / justiceMatt 5:6 (hunger and thirst for it); Rom 3:21-26
ἐκδικέω / ἔκδικος ekdikeo / ekdikosGreekTo vindicate or avenge; an avenger or one who executes justiceRom 12:19 (do not avenge yourselves); Rom 13:4 (the authority is "an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer"); Luke 18:3-8 (vindication for the widow)

The "eye for an eye" principle (Exod 21:23-25; Lev 24:19-20; Deut 19:21) functioned in its context as a limit on retaliation: the penalty may be no greater than the harm — a contrast to Lamech's escalating revenge. Jesus then reorients personal responses further (Matt 5:38-42): do not meet evil with retaliation. Interpreters debate how far Matt 5 reaches (whether it addresses only personal retaliation or also civil penalties); the text itself addresses what you do when wronged.

5.3 Why Revenge Is Not Justice

  • The victim is judge in their own case. Even honest pain distorts proportion; Scripture's whole legal framework removes this role (Deut 19:15-21; Rom 12:19).
  • It escalates. Feuds grow; each side feels its strike was justified response (Part 3.3).
  • It doesn't repair anything. The harm is not undone by a second harm.
  • It binds the victim to the offender (Part 3.3).
  • It makes the victim a second perpetrator, shifting the moral ground.

5.4 Why Punishment Alone Doesn't Heal the Victim

Restorative-justice writer Howard Zehr, whose Changing Lenses shaped modern restorative practice, reframes the question: ask not only "what law was broken and what penalty is owed?" but "who has been harmed, what do they need, and whose obligation is it to put things right?" What victims typically need goes beyond the offender's pain:

What victims commonly needDoes punishment alone provide it?
Truth: to know what happened and whyNot necessarily — trials and sentences can leave questions unanswered
Acknowledgment: to be believed and to hear "I wronged you"Rarely; a sentence is not an apology
Safety: to be protected from further harmSometimes (incapacitation, protective orders)
Voice: to be heard and to have a sayOften limited within adversarial processes
Restitution: material and practical repairSeldom directly
Meaning and closure: to make sense of it and move onNot reliably; the offender's suffering does not remove the victim's

What the research says (briefly).

  • Deterrence: the U.S. National Institute of Justice's summary of the evidence ("Five Things About Deterrence") states that the certainty of being caught deters far more than the severity of punishment, and that increasing severity does little to deter crime. This addresses deterrence only; it does not by itself settle whether penalties are deserved.
  • Victim outcomes: a Campbell systematic review (Strang, Sherman and colleagues, 2013) of randomised trials of face-to-face restorative-justice conferences found consistently higher victim satisfaction than conventional processing, and on average a modest but cost-effective reduction in repeat offending.
  • Limits: the evidence base concerns voluntary, carefully run conferences, mostly for particular types of offences and offenders; effects on repeat offending are modest; restorative processes can be unsafe or inappropriate where there is ongoing abuse or a serious power imbalance, and participation must never be coerced.

5.5 A Necessary Refinement: Is All Punishment Wrong?

No — and it would be dishonest to claim the Bible says so. Scripture gives civil authority a real role: the authority "does not bear the sword in vain; he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer" (Rom 13:4); Paul himself says he will not refuse the penalty if he has done wrong (Acts 25:11); the church exercises discipline (1 Cor 5; Matt 18). God's own judgment is affirmed (Rom 12:19; 2 Thess 1:6-7), and the martyrs' cry "how long, O Lord... will you not judge and avenge our blood?" (Rev 6:10) is not rebuked. So the defensible claims are:

  • Personal revenge is forbidden and does not heal.
  • Proportionate, protective consequences through legitimate processes can be just, and may be necessary for safety.
  • Punishment alone is not the whole of justice, and it does not by itself repair the victim.
  • Final judgment belongs to God.

Christians disagree on the deeper question. Many Reformed and other traditions hold that justice by its nature requires penalty — and that the atonement is precisely God satisfying that requirement in Christ (penal substitution). Anabaptist and other restorative traditions emphasise that biblical justice is aimed at making things right and reconciling, and read the cross as God absorbing the cost of putting the world right. The relational-gospel reading used in this series leans to the restorative emphasis while not needing to deny a civil role for consequences. Readers should weigh the difference as a real one.

5.6 The Motive Test: Justice-Seeking or Revenge-Seeking?

QuestionHealthy signWarning sign
What am I really after?Safety, truth, repair, prevention of harm to othersTheir pain, humiliation or loss
Would I be at peace if the outcome were repair without their suffering?Yes, mostlyNo — I need them to hurt
Am I willing to go through a fair process even if it may not go my way?YesNo — I want a result, not a process
Am I using true facts and proper channels?YesI exaggerate, recruit mobs or leak selectively
Do I think about them constantly?The matter occupies time only when action is neededIt occupies my mind daily
Could I still pray for their awakening?Honestly, slowly, yesThe thought disgusts me or I pray for their downfall

5.7 Where Anger at Injustice Goes: Lament

The imprecatory psalms (e.g., Ps 109; 137; 58) show what to do with the desire for retribution: say it to God, in full, and leave the sword with Him. They are not scripts for cursing people; they are models of honest rage handed over. Putting feeling into words is also physiologically regulating (see the heart-healing study). Jesus himself quotes the psalms of reproach (John 2:17; Rom 15:3) and cries out from the cross (Ps 22).

PART 6 — The Unrepentant Victimiser

This builds on the forgiveness-repentance-reconciliation study in this series (especially its decision matrix and Part 7.5). Here we add the practical edge: what actually to do, and what to expect.

6.1 Eight Moves

#MoveWhy
1Safety firstIf harm is ongoing or likely, distance, protective orders, and professional help come before any other step.
2Name the truth and get witnessesBeing believed is a core victim need. Keep dates, messages and records; tell trusted people; do not carry it alone.
3Use legitimate processes (legal, institutional, church with outside oversight)Consequences through fair process protect you and others; run the motive test (5.6).
4Release the debt (aphiemi)For your freedom, not their sake (Heb 12:15; the forgiveness study).
5Set boundaries scaled to riskFrom limited contact to no contact; boundaries govern your actions, they are not punishment.
6Grieve what will not be restoredLament the relationship, the years, the apology that may never come.
7Keep your heart soft"Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you" (Matt 5:44; Luke 6:27-28 — agapao: active goodwill toward their good, not trust and not proximity).
8Do not make your peace wait for an apologyAn apology is theirs to give; closure can be self-authored with God and community.

6.2 What to Expect: Unrepentant Responses and How to Meet Them

Their responseWhat it signalsYour response
Denies it happenedAvoiding accountabilityRely on records and witnesses; don't re-argue facts endlessly.
Minimises ("you're too sensitive")Re-assigns the problem to youRestate once, briefly; exit the debate.
Blames youBlame-shifting (Gen 3:12)Own any real part; decline the rest.
Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender (the pattern named "DARVO" by psychologist Jennifer Freyd)Defensive counter-attack, not repentanceExpect it; don't mistake the accusation for insight; rely on third parties.
"If I offended you, I'm sorry"Conditional, non-specific regret (metamelomai-type, see the forgiveness study)Neither accept as repentance nor reject cruelly; watch behaviour over time.
Demands your forgiveness quickly, perhaps quoting ScriptureUsing forgiveness to end accountability"I am forgiving in my own time before God; trust will depend on changed behaviour."
Recruits allies against youTriangulationKeep to facts with the safe people you've chosen; don't campaign.

6.3 God's Own Pattern With the Unrepentant

Notice how God himself handles it. In Christ He is "reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them" (2 Cor 5:19) — a finished release on His part — and yet the next verse says "we implore you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God" (5:20). He forgives unilaterally, pleads relentlessly, doesn't coerce, respects real consequences (Rom 1:24 "God gave them up"), and reserves final judgment to Himself. That is the pattern we imitate: release, plead where safe, wait, don't force, protect, and entrust. Part 7 develops this further.

6.4 Case Study: Vikram and His Elder Brother

Vikram (composite) discovers that his elder brother used forged signatures to move their late father's property into his own name. When confronted, the brother says Vikram "has always been jealous," tells relatives that Vikram is "creating trouble over money," and demands that Vikram "forgive like a Christian."

The pull of revenge. Vikram's first impulses: expose the brother to the extended family, post about it online, cut off their mother's contact with the brother's children. He recognises the urge as a revenge menu (Part 3.1: exposure, sabotage, displacement).

What he does. Safety is not a physical issue, so he focuses on moves 2-8. He gathers documents and consults a lawyer (3); he files a legal challenge to the transfer, not to humiliate his brother but to protect the estate and their mother's share (and applies the motive test — he is honestly willing to settle if the property is restored). He tells two trusted people the full story (2), and writes an unsent letter to his brother (3.4). He releases the debt in a prayer on a specific day: "I release the claim that he owes me an apology" (4). He limits contact to written communication about the case (5). He grieves the brother he thought he had (6). He prays, on and off, "Lord, wake him up" — not "Lord, destroy him" (7). He decides his peace will not wait on a confession (8).

DARVO along the way. The brother accuses Vikram of greed and betraying the family; Vikram, forewarned, doesn't take the bait in family gatherings and keeps to facts.

Outcome, honestly told. The court process takes two years; the transfer is partly reversed. The brother never apologises. Vikram's relationship with him remains cold and limited. Vikram says: "The judgment helped protect what was ours. The forgiveness is what freed me. The reconciliation never came — and I had to grieve that separately."

6.5 When the Victimiser Holds Power

A boss, pastor, parent or public figure who is unrepentant is harder, because power insulates. Use outside channels (regulatory bodies, denominational or independent oversight, legal advice), build a coalition of corroborating witnesses where safe, protect your income and safety first, and remember the safe-church marks from earlier in this series: separation of safety from reconciliation, outside accountability, and no pressure on the harmed person to meet the one who harmed them.
